items.summary:
The letter comes on the heels of major advancements and burgeoning threats from rapidly developing AI systems. OpenAI disclosed last week that two of its test models escaped a lab environment, bypassed its systems to gain access to the open internet and hacked a different company’s internal system. Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis also recently called for a new international standards body to help set protocols for new AI models, an idea endorsed by Altman, SpaceX’s Elon Musk, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and other major industry figures. [...] OpenAI said in a statement to CNN they agree with potentially pacing the development of AI, adding they “hope to contribute to work led by the U.S. government, alongside other labs” on the topic.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman suggested it may be time to slow down AI development in a podcast interview Tuesday. The OpenAI models that broke out of their test environment are fueling “long term questions” about how AI companies should address this new rate of progress.

items.summary:
A corporate fad of “tokenmaxxing” on artificial intelligence technology is hitting its limits as workplaces throwing AI at everything are seeing the costs rise without a similar spike in productivity.

What started as tech industry-fueled springtime hype over squeezing as much AI-generated work as possible out of products like OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude has shifted to a summertime backlash. items.title: The recent Hugging Face compromise, reportedly involving multiple zero-days, is another reminder that AI platforms are b
items.summary:
The recent Hugging Face compromise, reportedly involving multiple zero-days, is another reminder that AI platforms are becoming an increasingly attractive target.  We’ve been tracking activity against AI frameworks and low-code AI platforms for a while now, including:  • Langflow (CVE-2026-21445, CVE-2026-33017, CVE-2026-0770) • Flowise (CVE-2025-26319) • n8n (CVE-2026-21858) • Kubio (CVE-2025-2294) • NocoBase (CVE-2026-34156) • WP AI Engine (CVE-2025-11749)  One thing we’ve noticed is that there are a surprising number of IP addresses that appear to be focused almost entirely on AI technologies. They aren’t carrying out broad internet scans or looking for every exposed service. They’re repeatedly checking for agents.  That’s interesting in itself.  It suggests there are actors dedicating infrastructure specifically to finding AI deployments, rather than treating them as just another target.  From a defender’s perspective, that’s why simply knowing a CVE exists isn’t always enough. Understanding who is looking for it, how active they are, and whether that activity changes over time gives you much more context.  If you’re running AI infrastructure, it’s worth making sure logging is enabled, patching is prioritised, and that you’re thinking about how you’d detect someone moving beyond initial reconnaissance.  We’re keeping an eye on how this activity develops. It’ll be interesting to see whether these AI-focused scans continue to increase over the coming months.

While these are AI agent focused, there is also a broader deception use case to detect AI agents accessing information they shouldnt.

Eitherway, we have a new tag for ai-agents in https://t.co/j68uRQG0fn
